say: Drop a cat upside down, and somehow, it lands on its feet. Every single time? Almost.
In eighteen ninety four, a French scientist named Étienne-Jules Marey filmed a falling cat, frame by frame, at twelve frames per second.
And the photos looked impossible. The cat started with no spin at all, then flipped over in mid air, with nothing to push against.
Secret number one: a super bendy body. Cats have about thirty vertebrae and no locked collarbone, so they can twist like a towel.
Secret number two: the tuck and turn. The cat bends in the middle and tucks its front legs, so the front half spins fast while the back half barely moves. Then it swaps.
Kittens start showing this trick at three to four weeks old, and they have it down by about seven weeks.
Secret number three: cats are tiny parachutes. Spread out, a cat tops out around sixty miles an hour. A falling person? Around one hundred twenty.
But please don't test it. Cats still get badly hurt in falls. Vets even have a name for it: high rise syndrome. Keep those windows screened.
